video_title: Why the Post-Election Trade Unraveled | Protect the Pile Episode 31
gist: Hedgeye Asset Management PMs argue the post-election AI/market whipsaw was driven mostly by levered, factor-neutral hedge fund and retail leveraged-ETF flows rather than politics; data-center buildout will slow at the margin (not die) amid a Quad 4 comp setup, with a live debate over Anthropic's economics and memory's unsustainable margins. Oil is framed as a binary straddle between Iran-war capitulation and escalation.

insights.claim: As of Friday November 6, the S&P 500 was at about 7427, roughly 5% below its all-time high, while the equal-weight S&P had hit an all-time high just three days earlier and the 10-year yield was around 4.87%, back off its peak.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: The drawdown is concentrated in cap-weighted leaders, not broad market breadth.
insights.quote: S&P is at 7427 last time I looked, down 5% from the all-time high

insights.claim: The hosts had expected a 'blue wave' election result to sell equities off; futures did fall on election night, but S&P futures ripped the next morning, catching many off guard, before a significant selloff the following day.
insights.speaker: John McNamera
insights.so_what: Event-driven positioning around the election was wrong-footed in both directions within 48 hours.

insights.claim: A Goldman Sachs note reported that investors liquidated massive hedges into the post-election rally only to be forced to re-hedge during the next day's significant move lower.
insights.speaker: John McNamera
insights.so_what: Hedge-flow whiplash, not fundamentals, drove much of the week's volatility.

insights.claim: Sam Ramen argues the week's extreme daily moves (Wednesday's post-election rally, Thursday's drop) should not be over-interpreted as signals, and that investors should advance incrementally toward a longer-horizon goal rather than react to each swing.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Avoid extrapolating single-day moves in a flow-dominated market.
insights.quote: you can't read you know like the whole world's secrets in yesterday's move

insights.claim: RPK compares the 2026 post-election reaction to 2016, when futures tanked overnight as Trump's win became clear and then the market rallied the next morning, a reversal that also forced a famous Hedgeye call pivot.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Overnight election reactions have a history of reversing by the open.

themes.theme: Leverage, factor-neutral crowding and market structure

insights.claim: RPK describes today's market as dominated by quant, momentum/CTA and leveraged market-neutral long/short hedge funds all trying to factor-neutralize simultaneously, producing unstable, violent rotations as emergent behavior.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Crowded factor-neutralization makes rotations self-reinforcing and abrupt.
insights.quote: we built this system now that is a ton of quantitative, a lot of momentum

insights.claim: This week's violent rotations reportedly caused several hedge funds to shut down their equities books.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Forced de-grossing can extend dislocations beyond what fundamentals justify.
insights.quote: hedge funds are now shutting down their their equities books

insights.claim: Factor-neutralization relies on historical look-back correlations and common off-the-shelf risk models built on mean-reverting normal distributions, which fail precisely when correlations break down.
insights.speaker: John McNamera
insights.so_what: Model-driven risk management amplifies tail events instead of containing them.
insights.quote: They're just, you know, sometimes useful, right? But they're least useful when you most need them to be useful.

insights.claim: Per an FT article published the day the S&P peaked, hedge fund borrowing from banks has tripled since 2020; the top 15 hedge funds went from 8-9x leverage to about 12-12.5x, and funds ranked 16-50 went from roughly 2x to 4x.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Systemic leverage magnifies any wiggle in correlated factor books.
insights.quote: hedge fund borrowing from banks has tripled since 2020

insights.claim: John McNamera argues that since COVID leverage has migrated from tightly risk-managed pod shops (where a 5% drawdown gets you fired) to retail investors via leveraged ETFs, which lack rigorous risk controls and can trigger unprecedented forced liquidations.
insights.speaker: John McNamera
insights.so_what: Retail leveraged-ETF unwinds are a new source of forced selling.
insights.quote: leverage has migrated you know much more into the you know retail and everyday investor in the form of levered ETFs

insights.claim: Sam Ramen attributes Thursday's AI-trade selloff mostly to flows and market structure as funds got caught twice, with fundamental headlines (Democratic wins, a small European neocloud's news tied to Microsoft and Anthropic) merely adding fuel.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Flow-driven drawdowns may offer entry points if fundamentals are intact.
insights.quote: I think mostly flow and market structure and then these fundamental news headlines just kind of just kind of added more fuel to the fire.

themes.theme: AI infrastructure after the election: slower, not dead

insights.claim: Sam Ramen believes AI sentiment has swung from 'Super Bowl' to 'Super Bear' and has gone too far to the downside, without implying a return to euphoria.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Sentiment overshoot in AI may create selective long opportunities.
insights.quote: we've gone from like Super Bowl on that to like Super Bear and I I think we've swung too far

insights.claim: RPK dismisses the 'Democrats broke the AI trade' narrative, comparing data-center opposition to fracking politics: the buildout will happen if there is money and local tax base to be had.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Political headline risk to data centers is likely overstated.
insights.quote: I think this is fracking we love it makes for great politics to like light the water on fire

insights.claim: The new Democratic Texas governor's data-center platform (bring your own power, add power back to the grid, hire local union construction, build where communities agree) is seen as reasonable, and she has already softened her stance on permitted projects.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Texas policy shift is incremental, not a ban.
insights.quote: you bring your own power you don't use community border

insights.claim: Texas's decentralized governance limits the new governor's power: key bodies like the Public Utility Commission and Railroad Commission are staffed with prior-cycle appointees, and the state senate is fully Republican.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Structural checks blunt a sudden reversal of Texas data-center policy.

insights.claim: Sam Ramen estimates roughly 80% of big data-center projects are already under construction and unaffected, but 2029-2030 pipeline projects not yet permitted face delays, with marginal projects possibly dropping out and only 'blue chip' ones proceeding.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Out-year capex growth is at risk at the margin, hitting later-cycle orders.
insights.quote: 80% or so of these big projects are already under construction, that's not going to be affected

insights.claim: Governors across both parties recognize the U.S. lacks enough power generation and that electricity prices are too high, making power buildout a durable theme independent of AI data centers.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Power infrastructure retains long-tailed demand regardless of election outcomes.
insights.quote: we don't have enough power you know and we need to build power

insights.claim: Industrials captured little of the AI trade's upside but have worn all of its downside beta, reflecting the market pricing how one-time some of the capacity tightness is.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Industrial AI beneficiaries carry asymmetric downside beta.
insights.quote: they didn't give you all the beta of the upside, but then they're giving you tons of beta on the downside

insights.claim: RPK warns that marginal data-center growth has increasingly come from speculative builders rather than hyperscalers with real contracts and power, setting up a classic overbuild where capacity comes online at the worst time.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Speculative capacity raises odds of a future oversupply and capex bust.
insights.quote: that's a circular that's a circular firing squad because like you're all going to end up overbuilding

insights.claim: A slowdown of the data-center buildout would be the healthiest outcome, but Hedgeye flags a significant Quad 4 setup next year where tough comps on the capex boom will hit while earnings are still strong today.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: 2027 comps against the capex boom are a key headwind for AI-levered names.
insights.quote: you haven't even seen the tough comps yet like earnings are still amazing right now

insights.claim: RPK argues the Fed must be supportive for the AI capex boom to be comped; if the Fed fights it, it can't be sustained, and Goldman's raised 2027 spend estimates depend entirely on the financing outlook.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Monetary policy and financing conditions are the swing factor for AI capex.
insights.quote: the Fed has to be on your side to make this work

insights.claim: RPK says mapping Nvidia's financing commitments raises significant questions about how the AI buildout can be sustained.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Vendor-financing circularity is an underappreciated risk.

insights.claim: If 2028 data-center/power buildout comes in at, say, 45 GW instead of an assumed 50 GW, currently supply-constrained components (e.g., DRAM) could flip from balance to oversupply, and markets and industry will front-run that as prices roll over.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Small capex slope changes can flip commodity-like AI inputs into glut.
insights.quote: Oh but what if it's actually going to be 45?

insights.claim: Sam Ramen declares the 'everything trade' in AI he named a few weeks ago is over, expecting parts of the trade to enter long-term downtrends.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Shift from broad AI beta to selective exposure.
insights.quote: I called it the everything trade like a you know a few weeks ago. I think that clearly is is over.

insights.claim: Optical networking remains a fundamental bright spot because data centers are shifting from copper to optical switching, a penetration story moving from near zero to 100 over two to three years, increasing TAM capture per build.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Content-per-data-center winners can grow even if total builds slow.
insights.quote: you're going from copper to optical networking switches almost like from zero to 100 but that's going to happen over like two three years

insights.claim: If compute capacity gets pushed out, whoever owns existing compute capacity holds an asset that becomes more valuable.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Existing compute owners benefit from slower new supply.
insights.quote: whoever's got it now, that that asset is just gotten a lot more valuable

themes.theme: Anthropic and AI model economics debate

insights.claim: Sam Ramen, admitting it is a non-consensus view, is bullish on Anthropic after its S1, arguing it fuses a manufacturing model (cash-burning token factory with rising incremental margins) with a software model.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Anthropic's IPO economics may be misjudged by consensus.
insights.quote: I think right now if you think about anthropic it's like a manufacturing company

insights.claim: Sam cites that roughly 20-25% of Anthropic's leading-edge model was built by Claude, with each new model and its compute becoming more cost-efficient, creating operating leverage.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: AI-built AI compounds cost efficiency per token.
insights.quote: 20 25% of the the sort of leading edge model for anthropic was was built by

insights.claim: Sam predicts Anthropic will morph into a vertical-application company layering paid AI-native vertical apps on top of the base Claude subscription, akin to Amazon Prime's bundled add-ons, raising customer lifetime value.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Upsell bundle economics could justify premium valuation.
insights.quote: I think this company morphs into this vertical application company

insights.claim: RPK counters that at a $1.2-1.5 trillion valuation Anthropic is already priced as one of the most successful software companies ever, while Grok, SpaceX, Google and OpenAI will all pursue the same strategy and copy each other, pressuring pricing.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Competitive convergence may compress AI model and app economics.
insights.quote: Imagine if like Google didn't have a monopoly on search.

insights.claim: RPK notes AI models are currently selling a dollar for less than a dollar, being cash-flow negative, and that monetization pushes are already meeting usage pushback; he contrasts this with SaaS's inverted working capital that justified premium multiples.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: AI scaling metrics may overstate durable economics until cash generation appears.
insights.quote: if you sell a dollar for less than a dollar, you can scale really fast

insights.claim: RPK cites Palantir as an early example of an AI-era company that generates substantial cash flow.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Cash-generative AI names deserve differentiation.

insights.claim: Sam argues first-mover network effects (as with Google search) can create insurmountable leads even as the model layer commoditizes, and that value will migrate to the application layer.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Application-layer leaders, not model providers broadly, should capture value.
insights.quote: the model layer is commoditizing in front of our very eyes

insights.claim: Meta's Muse agent is good but cannot be rolled out globally due to insufficient compute, and is currently free to users, implying heavy subsidies that won't last.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Compute scarcity and subsidies constrain big-tech AI rollouts.
insights.quote: They can't roll it out globally because they don't have enough compute.

insights.claim: John compares AI competition to New York ride-hailing 15 years ago, when eight Uber-like services raced to the bottom (Wall Street to Upper West Side for $2) before consolidating into Uber with much higher prices; RPK notes even the bull case implies massive capital destruction among losers.
insights.speaker: John McNamera
insights.so_what: Expect consolidation and large capital destruction in AI before pricing power emerges.
insights.quote: I took rides from Wall Street to the Upper West Side for $2.

insights.claim: RPK describes himself as not an AI skeptic but an 'AI claim skeptic', believing the technology is transformative while doubting the claims embedded in valuations.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Separate technology adoption from investment returns.
insights.quote: I am not an AI skeptic I am actually an AI claim skeptic

insights.claim: RPK warns memory companies' roughly 90% EBIT margins are unsustainable (Google never achieved that) and low P/Es are a 'siren song'; he notes TSMC said Nvidia is asking it to build DRAM, and expects prices to fall toward normalized margins.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Avoid memory stocks on peak margins; new supply is coming.
insights.quote: 90% ebitar margins are not sustainable by anyone

themes.theme: Iran war, energy straddle and geopolitics

insights.claim: RPK says the week's energy selloff was driven by expectations of peace in the Iran war, following the vice president publicly blaming the war for the election loss within 24 hours.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Political pressure is tilting toward ending the war, weighing on oil.
insights.quote: it took 24 hours for the vice president to shiv the president on the Iran war

insights.claim: RPK frames oil as a 'straddle': the current price is wrong, with outcomes binary between capitulation (a hasty deal, floor below $95 but supported by inventory rebuilding and shipping cost curve) and escalation (renewed bombing sending prices sharply higher).
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Options-style positioning may suit energy better than directional bets.
insights.quote: there's capitulation or escalation there is no there is no middle way

insights.claim: China and India, both net energy importers, have resumed rising oil imports after half a year of conflict, signaling discomfort with drawing down inventories and greater incentive to push for resolution.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Importer pressure raises odds of a negotiated outcome.
insights.quote: China's imports have started to go back up again. India's imports are going back up.

insights.claim: Sam observes that Russia and China appear more involved in this round of Iran negotiations, possibly linking a Ukraine-Russia concession to Russian help on Iran in a three-way deal.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: A broader geopolitical bargain could accelerate de-escalation.

insights.claim: Israel's recent election appears to have weakened Netanyahu, potentially hamstringing his ability to drag the US into further escalation with Iran.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Reduces escalation odds in the oil straddle.

insights.claim: RPK argues Iran also wants the war to end since sanctions pressure is strangling its economy, and that it now has a 'scalp' from US political regime change, making this a good moment for it to seek a deal.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Both sides' incentives point toward capitulation over escalation.

insights.claim: A clock is ticking before the new Congress is seated (possible impeachment proceedings against 'hexag' (likely Hegseth), a carrier arriving in about a week), forcing a decision to escalate or withdraw, while the war becomes a fault line within the Republican party ahead of 2028.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK)
insights.so_what: Decision window for escalation is weeks, a near-term oil catalyst.
insights.quote: we do have a carrier that's going to be there in about a week
